title: FPRAS for counting perfect matchings
formal:
Does there exist one uniform probabilistic algorithm \(A\) and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every finite undirected simple graph \(G\) and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \(A(G,\varepsilon)\) halts on every random tape within
\[C\bigl(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+1\bigr)^{k}\]
Turing-machine steps and outputs a nonnegative rational \(\widehat Z\) satisfying
\[\Pr\bigl[(1-\varepsilon)Z(G)\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z(G)\bigr]\ge\frac34?\]
Here \(Z(G)\) is the number of perfect matchings, \(L\) is the complete input bit length defined below, and, whenever \(Z(G)=0\), every run must output zero. This is the existence question for a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme on general unweighted graphs.
definitions:
For every integer \(n\ge0\), a graph has labeled vertex set \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and an arbitrary subset of the unordered pairs of distinct vertices as its edges. It has no loops, parallel edges or weights. A matching is a subset of edges with pairwise disjoint endpoints; it is perfect when every vertex is incident to exactly one of its edges. Each such edge set is counted once, regardless of order or orientation. Thus \(Z(G)\in\mathbb N\), an odd-order graph has count zero, and the empty graph has count one, from its empty matching. The domain includes disconnected graphs, isolated vertices, odd cycles and arbitrarily large degrees, with no bipartiteness, density, planarity, expansion, or existence promise.

Use the following explicit finite encoding. The graph is encoded by \(1^{n}0\) followed by one adjacency bit for each pair \(0\le i<j<n\), in lexicographic order. This includes the full vertex set even when there are no edges and is polynomially equivalent to an explicit vertex-and-edge list. Write \(\varepsilon=r/s\) in lowest terms with integers \(0<r<s\). Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer, with \(b(0)=0\), and let \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Append \(E(r)E(s)\) to the graph encoding. The total length is \(L\); the numerical value of \(1/\varepsilon\), not just the length of its encoding, may enter the time bound. The output has the form \(E(u)E(v)\) with integers \(u\ge0,v\ge1\), meaning \(\widehat Z=u/v\); reduction to lowest terms is not required.

An algorithm is one finite multitape probabilistic Turing-machine program with a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes over fixed finite alphabets, and an output tape. Each ordinary transition and each newly requested independent fair bit costs one step. Its probability space is the infinite product of fair bits, and the clock bound must hold on every tape for every valid input. Reading, arithmetic, storage operations and writing the whole rational output are all charged. There is no advice, oracle, nonuniform dependence on the graph or accuracy, or unit-cost operation on unbounded integers. No guarantee is needed on malformed inputs. The same \(A,C,k\) must work for all graphs and all valid accuracies; success is per input and is not an average over a graph distribution.

The estimate has relative multiplicative error. In particular, an additive error guarantee on the raw count or on its logarithm is a different condition. Requiring deterministic zero output when no perfect matching exists is a harmless normalization of the usual FPRAS question because perfect-matching existence on general graphs is deterministically decidable in polynomial time. The probability \(3/4\) is fixed, and no random output is required to be an actual matching. This card asks whether the approximation algorithm exists; it does not ask for the numerical value of a fixed graph’s count at the catalogue’s default absolute tolerance.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition above or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a finite uniform algorithm and constants \(C,k\), and prove its every-random-tape clock, output encoding, exact zero behavior and per-input relative-error probability for every graph and rational accuracy. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm and every such polynomial bound; it need not consist of a single finite counterexample graph. Failure or slow mixing of a particular algorithm family does not prove that negation. A conditional impossibility theorem is only a conditional result unless its hypothesis is also proved. Exact exponential-time counting, constant-factor approximation without arbitrary requested accuracy, algorithms only for bipartite or dense graphs, and approximation of the total number of all matchings do not meet the target.
why: A canonical unresolved problem in approximate counting, separating efficient existence testing from estimating the number of solutions. It also controls the approximability of other counting and partition-function problems through reductions.

importance.reason: The major missing generalization of the permanent FPRAS, with an established obstruction to the direct Markov-chain approach and consequences beyond matchings.

progress.text: Jerrum–Sinclair establish an FPRAS for all unweighted matchings in arbitrary graphs, a neighboring count rather than unrestricted perfect matchings.
Jerrum–Sinclair–Vigoda give an FPRAS for nonnegative permanents; the checked author-hosted conference manuscript states the theorem, and the journal version appeared in 2004.
Štefankovič–Vigoda–Wilmes prove the stationary-mass-or-mixing obstruction for JSV-type chains and give approximation parameterized by factor-critical ear complexity; published at LATIN 2018.
Fei–Goldberg–Lu’s journal article includes the perfect-matching approximation equivalence and open-status statement; the checked arXiv v3 was posted on 17 August.
Chen–Vigoda–Yang v1 reports a faster permanent FPRAS with explicit accuracy and failure-probability dependence; the domain remains bipartite.
Yi v1 claims deterministic approximation for dense weighted hafnians with fixed degree and weight margins, and still lists unrestricted nonbipartite perfect-matching approximation as open.

status_note: Individually checked on 14 September 2026. General unweighted perfect-matching FPRAS existence is explicitly open in Štefankovič–Vigoda–Wilmes, Fei–Goldberg–Lu v3 (17 August 2025), and Yi v1 (3 September 2026). Chen–Vigoda–Yang v1 (27 August 2026) reports a faster permanent algorithm on bipartite graphs, while Yi’s new deterministic hafnian approximation requires a fixed positive density margin. Neither claims the unrestricted target. Their complete new proofs and implementations have not been independently verified. The 2017 lower bound concerns a specified Markov-chain family and gives a stationary-mass-or-mixing disjunction, not impossibility of every FPRAS. Bounded later-work searches found no matching full resolution; retained as source_open with these verification limits.

context_blocks.text: Finding a perfect matching is possible in deterministic polynomial time on general graphs, but exact counting is #P-complete even on bipartite graphs. A relative approximation can be much easier than exact counting, as the permanent demonstrates. This question asks whether that distinction persists on all simple graphs, making it one of the central missing cases in the theory of randomized approximate counting.

For an \(m\times m\) nonnegative matrix \(B\), its permanent is \(\operatorname{per}(B)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{m}}\prod_{i=1}^{m}B_{i,\pi(i)}\), where \(S_{m}\) is the set of permutations. When \(B\) is a zero–one bipartite adjacency matrix, the permanent counts perfect matchings between the two specified vertex classes. Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda prove an FPRAS for every nonnegative permanent, solving the bipartite matching case. Their theorem does not require the matrix entries to be strictly positive.

For a general graph on an even number of vertices, the corresponding expression is the hafnian of its symmetric adjacency matrix: the sum, over partitions of the vertices into unordered pairs, of the product of the selected entries. It is different from the permanent of that same square matrix. For example, \(K_{4}\) has three perfect matchings, but its adjacency matrix has permanent nine, because the latter also counts directed cycle covers. This example identifies the mathematical distinction between the two targets.

Jerrum and Sinclair’s 1989 Corollary 4.5 gives an FPRAS for the number of matchings of all sizes in arbitrary unweighted graphs. The related weighted monomer–dimer statement has a weight-encoding qualification; no unrestricted binary-weight theorem is needed here. Total matching count can differ exponentially from perfect-matching count: a disjoint union of \(j\) edges has \(2^{j}\) matchings but only one perfect matching. Thus the two quantities are not interchangeable even on elementary graphs.

Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes identify a precise obstruction for a family of chains on perfect and near-perfect matchings. A near-perfect matching leaves exactly two vertices uncovered, and its hole pattern records those vertices. For the specified JSV-type transitions and any weighting depending only on the hole pattern, their Theorem 2.2 gives graphs on which either perfect matchings have exponentially small stationary probability or the mixing time is exponential. The disjunction matters: the theorem does not assert slow mixing for every weighting, nor impossibility of every FPRAS. Their positive result treats bounded ear complexity of factor-critical subgraphs; a factor-critical graph remains perfectly matchable after deleting any one vertex, and ear count is not its vertex count.

The relevance extends to statistical counting models. Fei, Goldberg and Lu’s Proposition 1.2 recalls that, for fixed rational equal interaction parameters \(\beta=\gamma<-1\), approximation of the corresponding two-state spin partition function is equivalent to general perfect-matching approximation under reductions preserving the existence of an FPRAS. The source states this equivalence in both directions and explicitly identifies the perfect-matching question as open. Its other tractable parameter regimes therefore do not settle this one.

Chen, Vigoda and Yang’s preprint of 27 August 2026 reports an improved permanent FPRAS. For an \(m\times m\) zero–one matrix with \(m\ge2\), its Theorem 1 states time \(O(m^{6}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^{5}m\log(2/\delta))\) for relative error \(\varepsilon\) and failure probability \(\delta\); the trivial and zero-permanent cases are handled separately. The state space remains bipartite. This is a reported preprint running-time improvement within the solved neighboring case, not a general-graph theorem; its full proof and bit-level implementation were not independently verified here.

Zihong Yi’s preprint of 3 September 2026 claims a deterministic approximation scheme for weighted hafnians when the support graph has minimum degree at least \((1/2+\gamma)n\) and nonzero weights lie in \([\theta,1]\), for fixed \(\gamma>0\) and \(\theta>0\). The unweighted case takes \(\theta=1\), but it still has the fixed density margin. The polynomial’s exponents depend on these fixed margins. The paper explicitly retains the general nonbipartite FPRAS question as open and separately discusses its limitations at the exact Dirac threshold. The reviewed statement does not cover every graph, and the full new proof has not been independently verified.

A positive answer would extend a landmark success of randomized counting beyond bipartiteness. A negative answer would establish a separation between the ease of finding these objects and the existence of arbitrarily accurate relative estimates of their number. The source-specific Markov-chain obstruction explains part of the difficulty without deciding this algorithm-independent question.

sentences: A perfect matching pairs every vertex of a graph with exactly one neighbor.
The question asks for one randomized algorithm giving arbitrarily accurate relative estimates of their number on every finite unweighted simple graph.
Its worst-case running time must be polynomial in the full input length and inverse accuracy, with success probability at least three quarters for each input.
Bipartite perfect matchings and all matchings have approximation schemes, but the checked 2026 dense-graph and permanent results retain restrictions absent from this target.
A complete Lean proof must establish such a uniform scheme with exact zero behavior or prove that no scheme meeting all requirements exists.
